To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

with increasing age, the rate of pacemaker cells decreases in the atrium and ventricle of the heart, the rate of the atrial pacemaker decreases to a greater extent, and the adrenergically induced acceleration of the heart rate decreases in both the atria and ventricles.
with increasing age in the rat there is a decrease in heart rate in vivo, in vitro and in the pacemaker rate of both atrial and ventricles.
with age, the adrenergically induced increases in heart rate and pacemaker rate are decreased, and that this is due to changes in both pacemakers and the adrenergics nerves innervating them.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of aging on cardiac rate and on adrenergically-mediated changes in cardiac rate.
the role of the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) in the aging process.
the effects of age on the autonomic innervation of the heart in Fischer-344 (F344) rats and the role of adrenergic innervation in the age-related decline of cardiac function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
with increasing age in rats, the pacemakers in the heart are less responsive to adrenergic stimulation, and that the adrenergically innervated heart is less responsive to adrenoreceptor stimulation.
the age-related decrease in heart rate is due to a combination of changes in the heart and in the sympathetic innervation of the heart.
the age-associated decrease in heart rate is due to a decrease in both pre and postjunctional adrenergic activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
aging in rats is associated with decreased cardiac pacemaker activity which may be the result of changes in both the pacemakers in the heart itself as well as in adrenergically innervating nerves.
the age-associated decline in cardiac rate is a result of both pre- and postjunctional changes in the sympathetic innervation of the heart.
with age, there are changes in the heart and in the adreneric nerves innervateing the heart, and that the changes in the nerves contribute to changes in the pacemaker activity of the heart.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the adrenergically innervated pacemaker of the heart, the sinoatrial node, is more affected by age than the adrenergicamente un-innervated pacemaker, the AV node.
the age-related decrease in the cardiac pacemakers themselves (i.e. postjunctional changes) appears to contribute to the age-related decrease cardiac pacemaker activity and rate.
with age the heart rate decreases in part due to changes in pacemakers of both the atrium and ventricle and in part due to decreased sympathetic innervation.
